speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The first change relates to the transfer of awards between companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The Pioneer Industry award and Pioneer Service award are granted to companies to encourage them to locate “pioneering” products or activities that introduce advanced technology, skills or know-how to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Meanwhile, the Development and Expansion award encourages companies to grow capabilities and conduct new or expanded activities in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: As companies amalgamate, merge or undergo corporate restructuring, there may be a need to transfer their existing awards to the new entity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Under this framework, such award granted to the transferee will be treated as a continuation of the award granted to the transferor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: A corporate partnership refers to a partnership, limited liability partnership or limited partnership comprising solely of partners that are companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: The	IA	scheme	encourages	companies	to	carry	out projects with economic, technical or other merits, by providing an allowance granted at a specified percentage of qualifying fixed capital expenditure incurred on an approved project.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: However, the IA currently can only be awarded to a company, but not a corporate partnership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: We know that companies increasingly co-own assets with other companies, including through corporate partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: There are sound business reasons for having these partnership arrangements, such as co-sharing of equipment to reduce expenses and to optimise usage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: To better cater to the evolving business environment, clauses 6 and 7 of the Bill amend section 66 and introduce a new section 66A of the Act, respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This is to extend the IA scheme to include corporate partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Details to enable implementation will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: This will help strengthen Singapore’s position as a leading digital connectivity node.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
text: Clauses 6 and 8 of the Bill amend sections 66 and 67 of the Act, respectively, to give legislative effect to this inclusion.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, we are entering a new era of increasing volatility and disruption.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We are in the throes of the COVID-19 pandemic as we speak but I fear the climate crisis will unleash chaos and food supply disruptions that dwarf what we have seen.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet there exists enormous growth opportunities for technologies that the world needs to exit the climate crisis and enter a world of peace and stability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Is the EEIA able to attract the kind of investments and innovation that will allow Singapore to demonstrate climate leadership and ride on the low-carbon wave?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are two parts to this question that I hope the Minister can address.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: EEIA provides tax relief for pioneering economic activities as well as a wide range of capital investments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My first point, Mr Speaker, relates to whether the EEIA extends incentives to high-carbon activities so that the tax relief may end up as a subsidy to the fossil fuel industry.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean recently announced Singapore's goal of achieving net zero emissions "as soon as viable in the second half of the century".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Senior Minister Teo himself admitted that this goal is "very challenging".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet even this goal falls short of the target of net zero by 2050 that IPCC estimates would limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius and avert the worst impacts of climate change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To have even the slightest hope of meeting this target, we have to stop incentivising investments that will lock in decades of high carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This year’s Budget has already allocated $5 billion to the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It would be unthinkable if we gave out tax relief to the same activities that will force us to spend more on coastal and flood protection.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I would imagine this would give Deputy Prime Minister Heng a bit of a headache trying to balance the Budget.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify whether the qualifying criteria for tax relief under the EEIA considers the long-term impacts on Singapore?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, is there consideration for whether the activity would lead to an increase in carbon emissions?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: EDB has published its assessment criteria for pioneer certificate incentives under the EEIA, which includes employment created and spin-off to the economy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For high-carbon sectors, even such economic benefits are not assured.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In 2015, when oil prices fell below US$50 per barrel, the oil and gas sector cut an estimated 15,000 jobs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With oil prices bottoming out again this year, ExxonMobil has said it will make significant cuts to spending.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As climate action accelerates across the world, demand for fossil fuel products may reduce sharply.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, with countries around the world, including Singapore, moving towards full electrification of their land transport system, demand for diesel and petrol is expected to drop.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Researchers from Columbia University forecasted that passenger vehicle oil demand would decline beyond 2025.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For the lowest low-carbon scenario in their 2019 study, oil demand in this sector would decline from about 25 million barrels per day today to 10 million barrels per day in 2040.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Investments in fossil fuel assets which underestimate the downside risk of disruptions from low-carbon technology, energy efficiency and climate policy could lead to stranded assets.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify whether the economic benefits under the assessment criteria for EEIA tax relief includes consideration for the downside risk from future disruptions, such as decarbonisation?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, the global transition to low-carbon opens up a host of new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My second point, Mr Speaker, therefore relates to incentives for innovations and investments that are aligned with a carbon-neutral economy.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Section 67 of the EEIA currently lists activities eligible for investment allowances.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These include reducing consumption of water and improving energy efficiency.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, this leaves out a wide range of capital expenditure investments that contribute to Singapore's long-term sustainability, such as renewable energy, active mobility, as well as waste reduction.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While there are grants available for some of these activities, such as the 3R fund for waste recycling and reduction, this should not preclude the option to use investment allowances as an additional incentive.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify whether the list of activities eligible for investment allowances can include a category for capital expenditure that reduce greenhouse gas emissions either directly or indirectly?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For pioneering economic activities, aligning our tax incentives with a carbon-neutral economy would help us get a foothold into a host of emerging industries that support a climate-friendly future.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These industries include carbon capture and storage, renewable energy, circular manufacturing, bio-plastics, energy storage, electric vehicles, alternative meat, climate-resilient agriculture and green building technology.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Clean energy alone is expected to generate 2.2 million jobs in ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We are building one of the world's largest floating solar farms in Tengah Reservoir.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The expertise we develop would position Singapore as a key exporter of this technology.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An undersea cable to transmit solar power from Australia could also be in the pipeline.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Alternative meat start-ups Beyond Meat and Impossible Foods have already taken the world by storm.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A recent headline in TODAY read: "Singapore has been buttressing its food security for decades.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, it was because of decades of effort to diversify our food sources that allowed Minister Chan Chun Sing to welcome the 300,000 airflown eggs to Singapore from Thailand when the risk arose that supply of eggs from Malaysia could be affected by the overnight lockdown.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In that same spirit, let us have the foresight and courage to prepare our economy for the risks and opportunities that emerge from a carbon-constrained future.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Every tool in our policy toolbox needs to be on the table.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the Minister's response to my clarifications above.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Singapore's strategies to reduce carbon emissions are formulated at the national level through the inter-Ministerial committee on climate change, which has been formed since 2007.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And these in turn shape how we work with our companies and industries, both existing and new, to make the necessary adjustments to prepare for a carbon-constrained future.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will also evaluate if the investment contributes to Singapore's economy, advances our capabilities, and creates good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the area of the petrochemical industry, for example, this is an important sector for Singapore, in terms of both direct and indirect contributions to the economy, to jobs and to livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what we will do is we will work with the industry players to make sure that what we have in Singapore are best-in-class, because we do not just produce to meet Singapore's domestic needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our petrochemical industry actually serves the whole world, consumers in different parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we will work with them and implement measures that will meet best-in-class standards for this industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Singapore take our climate change commitments seriously because we know we need to do our part.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And hopefully this will also set a good example for other countries to do likewise.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I say this because climate change requires global action.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If the other countries do not follow suit, we will not be able to tackle this global challenge together.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when we invest in protecting our shorelines, this is something that we are investing to protect both the current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But in order for sea levels not to rise significantly, it is going to go beyond what Singapore can do alone.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is why we hope that the world can work together, to be able to find solutions and tackle climate change together.      .
